---
title: "Continuous-time stochastic models"
subtitle: "Otto & Day, chapter 15, with PracticalCAS"
engine: julia
---

In continuous time a Markov chain is described by rates. The probabilities of
the states obey linear ODEs, the Kolmogorov forward equations, solved by the
matrix exponential of the rate matrix. For large populations, allele
frequencies follow a diffusion: a mean change `M(p)` and a variance `V(p)` per
unit time determine fixation probabilities, absorption times and stationary
distributions.

```{julia}
using PracticalCAS
@syms t::nonneg
```

## A two-state chain in continuous time

A gene switches on at rate `α` and off at rate `β`. The rate matrix has rows
summing to zero; the transition probabilities are `exp(Q t)`:

```{julia}
@syms α::positive β::positive
Q = [-α α; β -β]
Pt = matexp(Q, t)
```

```{julia}
stationary_distribution(Q; continuous = true)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(Pt[1, 1], β / (α + β) + α / (α + β) * exp(-(α + β) * t))
@assert all(isequiv.(stationary_distribution(Q; continuous = true), [β / (α + β), α / (α + β)]))
```

## The linear birth–death process

Each individual gives birth at rate `λ` and dies at rate `μ`. The expected
population size follows `dm/dt = (λ - μ) m`:

```{julia}
@syms λ::positive μ::positive m::positive n₀::positive
dsolve(ode(m => (λ - μ) * m), t; ic = n₀)
```

The first event in a lineage is a birth with probability `λ/(λ + μ)`, so the
lineage of one individual is a branching process with offspring generating
function `(μ + λ s²)/(λ + μ)`. It escapes extinction with probability
`1 - μ/λ` when `λ > μ`:

```{julia}
@syms s
assuming(λ > μ) do
    extinction_probability((μ + λ * s^2) / (λ + μ), s)
end
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(dsolve(ode(m => (λ - μ) * m), t; ic = n₀), n₀ * exp((λ - μ) * t))
@assert isequiv(assuming(() -> extinction_probability((μ + λ * s^2) / (λ + μ), s), λ > μ), μ / λ)
```

The forward equations for a small birth–death chain on `{0, 1, 2}` (absorbing
at 0; births from 1 to 2, deaths from 2 to 1 and from 1 to 0) give the
probability of extinction by time `t`:

```{julia}
Qbd = [0 0 0; μ -(λ + μ) λ; 0 2μ -2μ]
P3 = matexp(Qbd, t)
simplify(P3[2, 1])
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
vals = Dict(λ => 1, μ => 1)
num = evalf(subs(P3[2, 1], vals..., t => 1.5))
# compare with a numerical solution of the forward equations
fw = simulate(ode(sym(:p0) => μ * sym(:p1), sym(:p1) => -(λ + μ) * sym(:p1) + 2μ * sym(:p2),
                  sym(:p2) => λ * sym(:p1) - 2μ * sym(:p2)), [0, 1, 0], 1.5; parameters = vals)
@assert abs(fw.u[end, 1] - num) < 1e-8
@assert abs(evalf(subs(P3[2, 1], vals..., t => 60)) - 1) < 1e-10

```

## Diffusion: fixation probabilities

With selection coefficient `s` in a population of size `N`, the allele
frequency has `M(p) = s p (1 - p)` and `V(p) = p (1 - p)/N`. Kimura's
fixation probability:

```{julia}
@syms p::(0, 1) σ::positive N::positive
u = diffusion_fixation(σ * p * (1 - p), p * (1 - p) / N, p)
```

A single new mutant (`p = 1/N`) in a large population fixes with probability
close to `2σ`:

```{julia}
taylor(limit(subs(u, p => 1 / N), N, ∞), σ, 0, 1)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(u, (1 - exp(-2N * σ * p)) / (1 - exp(-2N * σ)))
@assert isequiv(limit(subs(u, p => 1 / N), N, ∞), 1 - exp(-2σ))
@assert isequiv(taylor(limit(subs(u, p => 1 / N), N, ∞), σ, 0, 1), 2σ)
```

Without selection the fixation probability is the initial frequency (the
limit `σ → 0`):

```{julia}
limit(u, σ, 0)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(limit(u, σ, 0), p)
```

## Time to absorption

For a neutral allele the expected time until it is lost or fixed solves
`(V/2) T'' = -1` with `T(0) = T(1) = 0`:

```{julia}
T = diffusion_time(0, p * (1 - p) / N, p)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(T, -2N * (p * log(p) + (1 - p) * log(1 - p)))
@assert isequiv(simplify(p * (1 - p) / (2N) * diff(T, p, 2)), -1)
```

## Stationary distribution: mutation and drift

With mutation at rates `μ` (to `a`) and `ν` (back to `A`), the frequency never
settles, but its distribution does: a beta distribution.

```{julia}
@syms ν::positive
φ = diffusion_stationary(ν * (1 - p) - μ * p, p * (1 - p) / N, p)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(φ, p^(2N * ν - 1) * (1 - p)^(2N * μ - 1) * gamma(2N * (μ + ν)) / (gamma(2N * ν) * gamma(2N * μ)))
@assert isequiv(integrate(p * φ, p, 0, 1), ν / (μ + ν))
```

Its mean is the deterministic equilibrium `ν/(μ + ν)`:

```{julia}
integrate(p * φ, p, 0, 1)
```

## Simulation

Gillespie's algorithm simulates the birth–death process event by event. The
fraction of lineages from one individual that die out matches `μ/λ`:

```{julia}
@syms n
bd_events = [λ * n => [1], μ * n => [-1]]
outcome() = gillespie([n], bd_events, [1], 50.0; parameters = Dict(λ => 1, μ => 0.5), maxevents = 2000).u[end, 1]
extinct = count(iszero, [outcome() for _ in 1:2000]) / 2000
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert abs(extinct - 0.5) < 5 * sqrt(0.25 / 2000)
```

A stochastic SIR epidemic: in a population of 200 with `R₀ = 2`, some
epidemics fade out early and others infect most of the population.

```{julia}
@syms Sv Iv Rv b g
sir_events = [b * Sv * Iv => [-1, 1, 0], g * Iv => [0, -1, 1]]
finals = [gillespie([Sv, Iv, Rv], sir_events, [199, 1, 0], 500.0;
                    parameters = Dict(b => 0.01, g => 1.0)).u[end, 3] for _ in 1:300]
count(<(10), finals) / 300, maximum(finals)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert 0.3 < count(<(10), finals) / 300 < 0.7      # early fade-out ≈ 1/R₀
@assert maximum(finals) > 100
```
